case_study_insert.main_stem: Amberline Honey Farm (AHF) is a sole trader in the raw honey production and bottling sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2015 by Jessamine Cole, the business harvests and bottles raw unfiltered honey from 480 managed hives, selling through farmers' markets and its online honey club, operating a flat structure with autocratic leadership. AHF plans to invest $450,000 in a solar-powered extraction and bottling shed to supply its online honey club, financed by a $270,000 personal savings injection and a $180,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.60 a unit and a selling price of $8.40, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. AHF faces two problems: absenteeism during the late-summer harvest has reached 11%, and complaints about leaking caps are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Harvest and Bottling Log — Q3 2026: AHF harvested and bottled 21,500 jars last quarter; absenteeism during the late-summer harvest reached 11%, up from 7% a year ago. Cap-seal complaints fell from 26 to 14 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 2.9 days. A survey of 400 farmers'-market and online buyers found that 63% would pay up to $0.60 more for raw unfiltered local honey, and 46% would subscribe to a monthly honey club; the part-time harvest team needs overtime rota cover, and three harvest helpers have left since May. The owner is considering job rotation between hive work and the bottling shed to lift morale, and induction plus food-handler certification costs $260 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, the third rise this year, increasing the cost of overdrafts and other variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.95 to $13.73 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills for seasonal harvest staff working overtime. (3) Sugar and bee-feed costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, and food inflation is running at 7.4%, while consumer spending on local artisan food grew 5.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: AHF plans to fund the new solar-powered extraction and bottling shed with $270,000 personal savings and a $180,000 overdraft. Explain two advantages for AHF of using personal savings instead of relying on the overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Personal savings carry no interest charge, whereas the $180,000 overdraft would accrue interest from day one — and with the base interest rate now at 5.0%, overdraft costs are rising across the board. Every dollar saved on interest protects AHF's $4.80 contribution per unit and keeps the $450,000 expansion affordable for a sole trader whose entire livelihood rides on the harvest and the bottling shed paying for itself.

Point 2: Personal savings have no repayment deadline or withdrawal clause, unlike an overdraft that the bank can demand repaid or reduce at short notice — a serious risk while AHF's receivables have grown to $55,000 and its cash balance is only $38,000. Using $270,000 of savings keeps the overdraft undrawn for genuine emergencies such as a hive-collapse winter or a bottling-machine breakdown, and demonstrates to the bank that Jessamine Cole has committed her own funds, which strengthens any future negotiation for a longer-term loan to refinance the overdraft after March 2027.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Amberline Honey Farm and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: AHF is launching its raw unfiltered local honey through new channels. Consider expanding farmers' market stalls, the online honey club subscription, or supermarket in-store tastings. Which should AHF choose to grow sales? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Expanding farmers' market stalls: Farmers' market stalls suit raw honey's artisan image, let Jessamine meet the 63% of 400 surveyed buyers willing to pay $0.60 more, and generate impulse purchases from Saturday shoppers. Each stall, however, costs pitch fees, transport and — critically — staff time: with harvest absenteeism at 11% and three helpers gone since May, AHF cannot reliably staff three more weekend stalls, and sales are weather-dependent and capped by stall-day traffic rather than the 80,000-unit annual output AHF wants to sell.

Online honey club subscription: The honey club converts the 46% of surveyed buyers who said they would subscribe to a monthly club into recurring, predictable revenue with no pitch fees, and boxes can ship direct at a 2.9-day fulfilment time with the flat structure autocratically managed for tight dispatch. Subscriptions smooth seasonality between harvests, build a first-party customer list for new varietals, and fit the $450,000 shed's role as an online-fulfilment hub; the risks are packaging and postage costs, subscription fatigue, and needing reliable dispatch staffing during harvest.

Supermarket in-store tastings: Tastings in national supermarkets would put raw honey in front of mass shoppers and could win permanent listings that absorb large volumes fast — attractive given 80,000 units of capacity. However, supermarkets demand margins, slotting fees, strict delivery windows and often private-label pricing that conflicts with raw unfiltered premium positioning, and they would squeeze the $8.40 price and $4.80 contribution; AHF would also compete on shelf with mass honey brands capitalised for national advertising, which a 16-person sole trader cannot match.

Recommendation: AHF should choose the online honey club subscription. It aligns with the 46% subscription-willing segment and the 63% premium-willing buyers, creates recurring revenue that smooths the harvest cycle, costs far less than supermarket slotting fees or three extra staffed stalls, and fits the shed investment and the 2.9-day fulfilment operation; farmers' markets are rejected as the growth engine because absenteeism and helper losses make new stalls unstaffable and weather-dependent, and supermarket tastings are rejected because the listing margin and compliance burden would destroy the premium positioning and $4.80 contribution that fund the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the channel options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AHF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AHF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why farmers' markets and supermarkets are rejected.

questions.question_text: AHF's absenteeism during the late-summer harvest reached 11%. Explain two benefits for AHF of using non-financial motivators such as job rotation to improve attendance in its harvest team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation between hive work and the bottling shed breaks up repetitive, hot, sting-risk tasks that cause harvest workers to skip shifts; alternating roles satisfies workers' variety and esteem needs (Maslow) and makes each role feel fairer, which lifts attendance during the critical six-week crush when every absent picker directly reduces jars bottled of the 80,000-unit annual target.

Point 2: Rotation builds a flexible team that can cover capping, filling and labelling when someone is ill, reducing the disruption that 11% absenteeism causes to the 2.9-day fulfilment promise made to online honey club members. Because AHF is autocratic and flat, job rotation also gives Jessamine Cole a low-cost way to show she trusts and values the 16 staff, lowering turnover among the part-time helpers she has struggled to keep since May, without raising wages she cannot yet afford against a $3.60 variable cost. It also gives permanent staff a structured way to pass on cap-seal and fulfilment know-how to new helpers, embedding the quality push into the team rather than into Jessamine alone.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AHF's absenteeism, workforce and fulfilment performance.

questions.question_text: AHF is short of harvest hands. Consider paying overtime to the existing part-time team or recruiting two additional part-time harvest helpers. Which should AHF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Paying overtime to the existing part-time team: Overtime rewards loyal part-time staff who already know the hives, the extraction room and the cap-seal standard, avoiding recruitment, induction and the $260 food-handler certification per new helper; it can start this weekend and directly covers the absentees. However, overtime pay usually runs at a premium, quickly breaching AHF's $144,000 fixed-cost base, tired workers make more cap-seal mistakes (cap-seal complaints already fell from 26 to only 14 per month), and pushing the same sixteen staff harder at harvest risks deepening the 11% absenteeism problem rather than curing it, since fatigue is often why staff stay away in August.

Recruiting two additional part-time harvest helpers: Two extra helpers spread the harvest load, cut overtime premiums, give AHF cover for the 11% absence rate, and fresh capacity supports the cap-seal quality push and the online club's fulfilment promise; at $260 each the certification cost is only $520 and they can be trained via the owner's autocratic supervision and job rotation alongside the core team. Disadvantages are that two unknown recruits may not stay — three helpers have left since May — and supervision, equipment and insurance costs rise, while inexperienced hands can slow the extraction room during the critical six weeks.

Decision: AHF should recruit the two additional part-time harvest helpers and reserve modest overtime for the peak fortnight only. Recruitment spreads the physical load, protects cap-seal quality, keeps the online honey club dispatching on time, and costs just $520 in certification plus wages, whereas overtime-only reliance would overload the tired core team, worsen the 11% absenteeism and cap quality precisely when the $450,000 shed is launching; pure recruitment without any overtime is rejected too, because one helper will inevitably fall ill during harvest and a small premium-rate safety valve keeps the line moving without permanent headcount growth.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two staffing options with limited application to AHF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of both options in the context of AHF's absenteeism and harvest workload.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of AHF with a well-justified decision covering cost, quality, fatigue and certification.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how AHF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $144,000 ÷ ($8.40 − $3.60) = $144,000 ÷ $4.80 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $8.40 − $3.60 = $4.80. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.80.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways AHF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Jessamine Cole can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 80,000 units to confirm AHF is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 50,000 units, which supports approving the $450,000 shed and the online honey club rather than delaying the investment.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.80 lets AHF model the $0.60 premium that 63% of surveyed buyers will pay: raising price to $9.00 lifts contribution to $5.40, so managers can forecast exactly how many extra jars of the raw unfiltered range must sell to keep total contribution unchanged.
3. Fixed costs of $144,000 and contribution per unit can be used to stress-test the $180,000 overdraft against late honey-club renewals or a weak harvest, confirming how many units above break-even are needed before the overdraft is comfortably serviced and refinanced as a term loan.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($144,000 ÷ 80,000 units + $3.60 = $5.40 a unit) to benchmark harvest-to-bottle performance each quarter, price the subscription box profitably, and judge whether job rotation or the two new part-time helpers deliver better output per $1 spent during the 11% absenteeism squeeze.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.80 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 50,000 units against 80,000-unit output; premium-pricing modelling from $4.80 contribution; overdraft stress-testing on the $450,000 expansion financed by $270,000 personal savings; and unit-cost benchmarking at $5.40 to manage the 11% absenteeism and subscription pricing.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AHF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Which judgement do the figures support — has AHF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.47 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.94 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.68 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.16 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $75,000 inventories + $40,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $140,000; 2025 current assets = $62,000 + $55,000 + $38,000 = $155,000. Short-term coverage 2024 = $140,000 ÷ $95,000 = 1.47; 2025 = $155,000 ÷ $80,000 = 1.94. Quick coverage excluding inventories 2024 = ($140,000 − $75,000) ÷ $95,000 = $65,000 ÷ $95,000 = 0.68; 2025 = ($155,000 − $62,000) ÷ $80,000 = $93,000 ÷ $80,000 = 1.16.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved markedly. The coverage of immediate debts rose from 1.47 to 1.94, helped by current liabilities falling from $95,000 to $80,000 and cash rising to $38,000. The quick coverage improved from 0.68 to 1.16 — a move from dangerous reliance on selling honey to meet debts, to comfortable coverage without touching stock, which is vital while a $180,000 overdraft is partly funding the shed. However, receivables rose from $40,000 to $55,000, suggesting wholesale or club customers are paying later and tying up cash just as the overdraft lingers; and inventories fell from $75,000 to $62,000, an efficient cut but one to watch if the harvest underdelivers or online orders spike after the club launch. Relying on an overdraft at a 5.0% base rate remains the weakest part of the funding mix, and refinancing to a term loan post-expansion would strengthen the position further.

Conclusion: AHF's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.47 to 1.94) and the acid test ratio (0.68 to 1.16) show stronger short-term solvency without depending on inventory sales, and the improvement is backed by falling liabilities. The residual risks are the rising receivables and overdraft-funded expansion, so AHF should tighten club and wholesale payment terms, refinance the $180,000 overdraft into a secured loan once the shed is operational, and set a target to keep quick coverage above 1.0 through the April 2027 wage change.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether AHF's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for AHF of launching the online honey club subscription.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The online honey club locks in recurring monthly revenue from the 46% of 400 surveyed buyers who would subscribe, smoothing the feast-or-famine harvest cycle and letting AHF plan jar production, staffing and the part-time rota around predictable demand. It also captures the 63% premium-willing buyers who will pay up to $0.60 more for raw unfiltered local honey, at a 2.9-day fulfilment time, with zero pitch fees or supermarket slotting charges, and it builds a direct customer list for future varietal launches alongside the $450,000 shed.

Disadvantage: Subscriptions add packing, postage and customer-service costs to every monthly box, diluting the $4.80 contribution if the $0.60 premium is not accepted; failed deliveries or cap-seal leaks — complaints fell only to 14 per month — trigger refunds and cancelled subscriptions quickly. The club also depends on reliable dispatch during the worst of the harvest when absenteeism sits at 11%, and subscription revenue can sag after the initial launch wave unless Jessamine adds variety, so cash planning must not assume every launch signup renews.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AHF's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in sugar and bee-feed costs will affect AHF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): AHF funds the $450,000 shed partly through a $180,000 overdraft, so a 0.75-point rise adds roughly $1,350 a year in interest directly, and any refinanced overdraft will also price higher. The bigger risk is strategic: with only $38,000 cash and $55,000 receivables, AHF cannot afford prolonged reliance on expensive overdraft funding, so the rate rise accelerates the need to convert the overdraft to a fixed-rate term loan backed by Jessamine Cole's personal guarantee once the shed is operational. Cash impact is real but small relative to payroll.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.73 per hour): AHF employs 16 staff including a part-time harvest team already needing overtime rota cover. A 6.0% rise adds roughly $1,600 per full-time worker — across the 16-strong workforce, roughly $25,000 to $30,000 a year in extra wages including harvest overtime premiums. This lands directly on the thin $3.60 variable cost and the $144,000 fixed-cost base, and it coincides with the shed launch, when Jessamine needs harvest productivity most to meet online honey club dispatch slots; absenteeism at 11% could worsen if pay fails to keep pace with the April 2027 rate.

Input cost inflation (9.4% sugar and bee-feed): Bee feed is used to sustain weak colonies through dearth periods and winter, and sugar syrup supplements late-season flows; a 9.4% rise adds real but bounded cost — on an apiary budget plausibly $25,000 to $35,000 a year, roughly $2,400 to $3,300 extra — far smaller than payroll, though it compounds if weak hives increase after a poor season and coincides with food inflation of 7.4%, pressuring price points.

Conclusion: The 6.0% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It adds roughly $25,000 to $30,000 a year to AHF's payroll across 16 staff, it is unavoidable, it lands during the shed launch and honey club ramp-up, and it hits the same harvest team whose 11% absenteeism already strains output. The 9.4% bee-feed rise is the second most serious pressure but is bounded by scale and can be partly offset by reformulating feed and colony management; the interest-rate rise is the smallest at roughly $1,350 a year on the overdraft and can be eliminated by converting to a term loan — so AHF should reprice its subscription plan modestly, push for the $0.60 premium, and refinance the overdraft before April 2027.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to AHF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AHF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AHF with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
